subtitle: People hold different expectations about authority, respect and participation. Examine those expectations with care, especially in hierarchies, while keeping actual responsibilities clear.
scope: For staff across DHS. Original practice cases support cultural understanding and suitable participation; they do not classify people, create decision authority or decide a complaint. Participation in this learning is voluntary. Actual agency duties and procedures remain. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: A question to someone in authority can carry different meanings. For one person, waiting for an invitation honors the role. For another, raising a relevant concern shows responsibility to the work. Power distance is one cultural concept that can help make those expectations visible. It does not establish a person’s motives or the authority of a real role. Explore an original community-choir case, optional private reflection and a separate DHS work situation.

intro.heading: Separate cultural expectations from actual authority
intro.body:
Power distance is a cultural concept about how unequal power is accepted and expected. Hofstede’s public explanation focuses on the less powerful members of organizations and institutions, including families. The concept can help you examine expectations about hierarchy, authority and who is invited to speak. It does not tell you whether a particular authority is lawful, whether an employee is capable or whether a person’s quiet response means agreement.

Hofstede’s national-culture comparisons concern broad patterns and include variation within countries. A country-level description is not a personal assessment. You cannot determine a colleague’s power-distance category from a name, accent, citizenship or posture. This course uses no national scores or rankings. It asks what a particular act means and which responsibilities apply in a particular setting.

Cultural expectations and actual authority also differ. A person might expect an elder, supervisor or director to decide, but that expectation does not establish the formal scope of the role. Someone might be invited to question a plan without receiving the authority to approve it. Conversely, a valid decision role does not make every method of participation unchangeable. You need the actual task and process rather than an assumed cultural rule.

The example concerns a community choir. Director Mira is responsible for selecting the sequence of songs in this project. During rehearsal, member Lena notices that two instructions conflict and waits. Member Bo raises a question before the next song. Those visible actions do not prove that Lena lacks ideas or Bo rejects direction. Their learned meanings have not yet been supplied.

A useful starting point is to identify the question and the role. What conflicting instructions were given? Does Mira want clarification before the next song? How do Lena and Bo understand a respectful way to raise the concern? Those questions can improve understanding without treating a framework as an answer about either person. Mira’s stated sequencing responsibility remains distinct from their participation.

You may also examine a private memory of being invited to speak or expected to wait. Consider what the invitation or waiting meant, not where you should be ranked. No history needs to be entered or shared. The example offers a complete alternative for learning the distinction.

flashcards.back: In Hofstede’s framework, the extent to which less powerful members of organizations and institutions accept and expect unequal distribution of power. It concerns cultural expectations, not a person’s score.
A relationship of roles or positions with different responsibilities or authority; its actual scope must be known.
What a person has learned a respectful act means, such as waiting to be invited or offering a relevant question.
A way to contribute or raise a concern; it does not automatically transfer the authority to decide.
The actual role and process for making a particular decision, rather than authority presumed from confidence, title or cultural expectation.
The meaning given to an act, which may need to be checked against the person’s explanation.

items.title: Keep the definition precise
items.body: Power distance concerns acceptance and expectation of unequal power. It is not simply the presence of a supervisor or a person speaking softly. In the choir, the existence of a director does not establish the members’ cultural expectations or explain why one member waits and another asks a question.

items.title: Check the actual role
items.body: Mira’s supplied responsibility concerns song sequence in this practice project. It does not establish authority over every member’s personal choice or every choir arrangement. Keeping the particular role visible allows a clarification question to be considered without assuming either unlimited power or no decision responsibility.

items.title: Describe the act without its assumed motive
items.body: Lena waits and Bo asks before the next song. Those are available acts. Calling Lena passive or Bo disrespectful adds an unsupported interpretation. A question about the meaning can supply useful information; a cultural category guessed from identity cannot.

tabs.label: Cultural expectation
tabs.body: A cultural expectation concerns what an act of hierarchy or respect is understood to mean. The framework may help identify that question. It cannot determine the full authority of the director or establish how a particular member interprets every instruction.

tabs.label: Actual responsibility
tabs.body: The example supplies Mira’s sequencing role. That is a fact about this project’s arrangement, not a country profile. Members can clarify conflicting instructions without automatically becoming the sequencing decision-makers. A real role would require its own actual authority and process.

tabs.label: Personal judgment
tabs.body: A conclusion that Lena lacks confidence or Bo rejects leadership would exceed the available acts. Such a judgment can hide relevant meaning and discourage useful clarification. It should not be treated as evidence about ability, attitude or an individual’s cultural orientation.

check.question: What does the opening example establish?
check.correct: Mira has the supplied sequencing responsibility, Lena waits and Bo asks; their meanings still need to be understood.
wrong: Lena’s silence proves agreement with both instructions.
Bo’s question proves disrespect for every authority.
The director role establishes each member’s power-distance category.
check.feedbackCorrect: This keeps the actual role and visible acts separate from meanings and personal conclusions that have not been established.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Silence does not establish agreement with conflicting instructions. One question does not prove a general attitude toward authority. A role cannot supply the cultural category of everyone around it. Each distractor turns limited observations into a personal conclusion without the needed evidence.

items.text: The concept concerns accepted and expected inequality of power.
A society-level comparison is distinct from a personal assessment.
Mira selects the song sequence in this project.
Bo asks about the conflicting instructions.
Lena’s pause proves a lack of ideas.
Bo rejects every director’s authority.

lessons.statement: Learn what respect expresses before deciding how to invite a contribution.

intro.heading: Understand two meanings of respectful participation
intro.body:
The example now supplies two learned meanings. In Lena’s early music lessons, a teacher first finished an explanation and then invited questions. Waiting for that invitation meant giving attention to the teacher’s work and not making the person lose the thread. Lena is waiting for a similar opening at rehearsal. Lena has noticed the conflict and wants it clarified; the pause is not an absence of a view.

Bo learned in a small community ensemble that raising a relevant uncertainty before singing helped the director and other singers. A question meant taking responsibility for a shared performance rather than allowing preventable confusion. Bo is trying to help Mira use rehearsal time well. Bo is not claiming the right to choose the songs or dismiss the director.

Before hearing the explanations, Bo saw Lena’s waiting as disengagement. Lena saw Bo’s early question as an interruption that challenged Mira. The meanings the people describe give each a reason to revise that reading. Bo can see attentive waiting; Lena can see a contribution intended to support the director. Their particular accounts do not establish what every student, teacher or choir member expects.

Mira can consider a clearer invitation: finish the short explanation, then explicitly ask for questions before the song begins, with another suitable opportunity to raise an unresolved concern. That option responds to Lena’s expectation of an invitation and Bo’s concern about preventable confusion. It leaves Mira responsible for the actual sequence while allowing meaningful clarification. It is a possible arrangement for this example, not a mandatory method for all rehearsals or DHS meetings.

The point is not that waiting is always respectful or questioning is always constructive. The content and timing of a question still matter. An invitation should make room for the relevant uncertainty rather than demand a cultural biography or praise every interruption. Understanding what the act means helps people choose a suitable response to the actual situation.

You may privately compare the two interpretations. You can recognize why an invitation matters without disclosing a personal memory or producing a workplace improvement. If you choose to discuss an actual situation, invite only what a person wishes to explain and preserve the applicable roles and responsibilities.

items.title: Read waiting with its supplied meaning
items.body: Lena’s explanation shows attentive waiting for an expected invitation. Asking “Did you have a question when the instructions differed?” can make that contribution visible. Calling the pause proof of disengagement would miss the meaning and the information Lena had already noticed.

items.title: Read questioning with its supplied meaning
items.body: Bo explains the question as helping prevent confusion before the group sings. That account changes the initial interpretation of a challenge to authority. The question can still be checked for relevance and timing; understanding the meaning does not make every possible interruption useful.

items.title: Make the invitation explicit
items.body: Mira can finish the explanation and ask for clarification before beginning. That opening responds to both meanings while preserving the director’s sequence responsibility. A clearer invitation is an adjustment to participation, not a transfer of every decision or a guarantee that all members will speak.

tabs.label: Assume quiet agreement
tabs.body: Treating Lena’s waiting as agreement would lose a relevant question about conflicting instructions. It would also substitute a convenient interpretation for the supplied explanation. A clear invitation can reveal the question without requiring Lena to defend a personal identity.

tabs.label: Assume hostile challenge
tabs.body: Treating Bo’s question as rejection of Mira would ignore the stated intention to prevent confusion. The better inquiry concerns the question’s content and how the invitation can work. It does not require declaring all spontaneous questions correct or removing the director’s responsibility.

tabs.label: Invite clarification clearly
tabs.body: An explicit question opportunity after the explanation can fit both concerns in this case. Lena has a recognizable opening, and Bo can raise uncertainty before singing. The arrangement can be checked with members without assigning them cultural categories or promising complete agreement.

check.question: What is a meaning-informed response in this case?
check.correct: Consider an explicit clarification opportunity after Mira’s explanation and before singing, while preserving the actual sequencing role.
wrong: Require Lena to speak immediately to prove confidence.
Ban Bo’s questions because they must be hostile.
Make every member the director so hierarchy disappears.
check.feedbackCorrect: The option connects the meanings the people describe to a concrete invitation without changing the actual decision responsibility.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Compulsory speech does not establish confidence or respect Lena’s meaning. A blanket ban misreads Bo’s supplied concern and can preserve confusion. Making everyone a director does not follow from the clarification need. Each shortcut changes the situation without responding to the actual meanings and roles.

items.text: Lena learned that waiting for an invitation honors the explanation.
Bo learned that a timely relevant question supports the shared performance.
Invite questions explicitly before the song begins.
Clarify that questions do not replace Mira’s sequencing responsibility.
Require a family history before allowing a question.
Treat speaking immediately as the only proof of respect.

responses: This changes the invitation in light of the meanings the people describe without forcing disclosure or transferring the role.
The task does not require a personal history, and the example’s explanations are enough for learning.
A pause can have different meanings and cannot supply that conclusion.

move.failure: An apparent improvement requires compulsory disclosure or treats one form of respect as universal.

takeaways: A learned expectation can be examined without judging your earlier self.
Personal cultural understanding has value alongside practical application.

lessons.statement: Make room to understand a familiar expectation without ranking yourself.

intro.heading: Examine your own learned relationship to authority
intro.body:
In this example, Ari recalls asking a school teacher a question after the lesson rather than during it. In that classroom, waiting meant respecting the whole group’s time. Ari later joined a workshop where the instructor explicitly welcomed questions during an explanation. Ari initially heard that invitation as a test rather than genuine permission. The memory shows how a familiar expectation can shape the interpretation of a new invitation.

Ari can examine both the learned meaning and the current context. Waiting in the first classroom was connected to a particular concern about shared time; the later workshop supplied a different invitation. Understanding the contrast does not require deciding that the first teacher was wrong or that Ari is permanently deferential. It can make the present choice easier to understand without rewriting every earlier relationship.

You may consider a private memory involving a teacher, coach, mentor, family relationship or another meaningful role. What did speaking, waiting, asking privately or disagreeing signify to you? How was that meaning learned? You need not select a painful experience or explain it to anyone. You may simply use Ari’s example. Neither route asks you to locate yourself on a country scale or an IDI assessment.

A worthwhile outcome might be recognizing a value: consideration for others, responsibility to a shared activity, respect for experience or the importance of having a voice. You may notice two values that remain in tension. That understanding is legitimate even if you make no immediate change and produce no work output. Cultural growth does not need a productivity receipt or a public confession.

If you want to consider a new response, begin with the actual invitation and responsibilities now present. Ari can ask the workshop instructor whether a question is welcome at that point. That small clarification differs from assuming that every teacher wants the same response. The old meaning can remain part of Ari’s understanding without controlling every new situation.

Personal reflection and an actual agency duty also remain distinct. Understanding a learned expectation cannot decide a service authorization, a legal obligation or a reporting response. When those matters arise, use the real requirements and appropriate process. For this lesson, an unrecorded explanation of Ari’s contrast is enough.

lessons.keyStatement: Make room to understand a familiar expectation without ranking yourself.

items.title: Name a value rather than a defect
items.body: Ari’s waiting expressed consideration for the class’s time. Naming that value provides a more accurate starting point than calling the earlier self timid. It leaves room to consider how the same value could be expressed under a different invitation without shaming a past choice.

items.title: Compare contexts before generalizing
items.body: The classroom and workshop supplied different participation expectations. Ari’s earlier response does not prove a permanent preference for silence. Examining the invitation, relationship and task can show why a new response might fit while avoiding a broad claim about every authority.

items.title: Let understanding be sufficient
items.body: A learner might privately understand a tension between consideration and having a voice. That insight can remain worthwhile without a shared story or immediate action. The example supplies an alternative, so learning does not depend on disclosing family experiences or agreeing to transform them.

tabs.label: A fixed self-label
tabs.body: “I am a high-power-distance person” would reduce several possible meanings and contexts to a label this course cannot establish. It could make a new invitation seem predetermined. A specific account of what waiting meant gives more useful understanding without claiming an assessment result.

tabs.label: A private reflection
tabs.body: “Waiting meant considering the class’s time; this instructor now invites questions during the explanation” preserves the context and meaning. Ari can understand that difference without recording it. A change may be considered, but the reflection has value even before a work action follows.

tabs.label: A forced change
tabs.body: Demanding that Ari challenge an authority to prove learning would replace one expectation with another compulsory performance. It could overlook the actual task and relationship. Reflection should support understanding and choice, not require conflict, disclosure or a demonstration of a new personality.

check.question: What is a legitimate result of Ari’s reflection?
check.correct: Understanding why waiting once expressed consideration and why a different invitation may offer another suitable response.
wrong: Assigning a permanent national-culture category to Ari.
Proving learning only by publicly challenging the instructor.
Declaring the earlier teacher and every similar authority disrespectful.
check.feedbackCorrect: The result keeps the learned value and current invitation visible without requiring a score, conflict or a universal judgment.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The course cannot assign a permanent category. Public challenge is not the only evidence of learning and need not fit the situation. One contrast does not establish the character of all earlier authorities. Each alternative turns reflection into a forced classification or judgment instead of understanding a particular meaning.

items.text: Ari connected waiting with consideration for class time.
The workshop instructor invites questions during explanations.
Consider how the invitations and relationships differ.
Explain the contrast privately using Ari’s example.
Reveal a family conflict to complete the lesson.
Create a workplace metric to make the reflection worthwhile.

lessons.summary: Distinguish an invitation to raise a question from the responsibility to choose the song sequence.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an invitation to raise a question from the responsibility to choose the song sequence.
objectives: Distinguish an invitation to raise a question from the responsibility to choose the song sequence.
Identify what a clearer invitation does and does not resolve.
Choose a response that preserves a relevant unresolved concern.
takeaways: Participation can inform a decision without making every contributor the decision-maker.
An invitation needs a recognizable opportunity and a way to clarify its meaning.
Unanswered content remains open even when the interaction feels more respectful.
lessons.statement: Make the contribution possible and keep the decision responsibility honest.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Clarify participation and the decision itself
intro.body:
Mira tries the revised rehearsal arrangement. After explaining the next section, Mira says, “Before we sing, what needs clarification?” Lena asks whether the printed repetition or the spoken instruction should be followed. Bo explains the same uncertainty from a different part of the choir. Mira identifies the intended instruction and clarifies it. The example supplies a question that was raised and answered; it does not supply every member’s experience.

The invitation improved this exchange because the opening was explicit and came before the singers needed the answer. It responded to Lena’s learned expectation of an invitation and Bo’s concern about preventing confusion. A welcoming phrase alone would have been less useful if Mira had immediately started the song or treated clarification as disloyalty. The response needs to be considered alongside the actual opportunity to use it.

That participation did not transfer Mira’s supplied sequencing role to the group. A member might have a recommendation about sequence, and Mira can explain how it will be considered under the actual project arrangement. Asking a question, having the question heard and controlling the decision are different. Calling them all participation can hide an important distinction.

An unresolved concern also should not be described as answered merely because the exchange was warm. Suppose a member asks how the written instruction will be corrected for the next rehearsal. Mira says that will be checked later. The question remains open. A useful account can acknowledge that the immediate instruction was clarified and keep the later correction visible without promising an answer that has not been given.

The cultural concept helps examine expectations around the invitation. It does not establish that every good process eliminates hierarchy or that every decision must be voted on. Nor does it justify an authority dismissing a relevant concern. The actual task, responsibility and available ways to contribute still matter. Clarifying those distinctions can reduce the need for participants to guess what a question means.

For private practice, explain how a contribution could be heard without being adopted. Consider a suitable account that names both the clarification and the unresolved written correction. You do not need to run a real meeting or publish a staff record to understand those distinctions.

items.title: Make the opening usable
items.body: Lena could ask before the group needed the instruction. That timing and explicit invitation matter alongside a friendly tone. If Mira invited questions while immediately beginning the song, the words alone would not establish a useful opportunity or show that everyone could use it.

items.title: Distinguish hearing from deciding
items.body: Bo’s question helps identify an uncertainty. It does not automatically establish the right to select the song order. A truthful explanation of how questions and recommendations will be considered preserves contribution while making the actual decision role understandable.

items.title: Keep the unanswered correction visible
items.body: The immediate singing instruction is clarified, but the later written correction remains a question. Recording both states avoids false completion. A considerate exchange is valuable, yet it cannot supply an answer, deadline or responsible commitment that was not actually given.

tabs.label: A question is heard
tabs.body: A contribution may be acknowledged and examined without being adopted as a recommendation. The account should explain what happened rather than imply that being welcomed transferred the decision. In this example the clarification had an answer; a different recommendation could remain under consideration.

tabs.label: A decision is made
tabs.body: Mira clarifies the intended instruction within the supplied role. That establishes a particular response, not unlimited authority over every question. The sequence responsibility and the members’ opportunity to seek clarity can coexist without treating each as the other.

tabs.label: A concern remains
tabs.body: The written correction for a later rehearsal is not yet established. Keeping it visible does not negate the useful clarification already given. It preserves what another conversation may need to address without presenting warm interaction as complete resolution of the content.

check.question: What does the revised exchange establish?
check.correct: The immediate instruction was clarified through a usable question opportunity; the later written correction remains separate and open.
wrong: Every choir member now controls the song sequence.
Every possible participation concern is resolved because the invitation was warm.
The unanswered written correction erases the useful immediate clarification.
check.feedbackCorrect: This describes the particular contribution and answer while retaining the actual role and unfinished concern.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A clarification question does not transfer the sequence responsibility. A warm exchange cannot establish every participant’s experience or answer every issue. One remaining question does not erase the useful answer already supplied. Each overstatement confuses the scope of the observed exchange.

items.text: Lena asked about the conflicting instruction.
Mira clarified what should be sung next.
The later correction of the written instruction needs checking.
Other members’ experiences were not supplied.
Everyone became the sequencing decision-maker.
Warmth proves that all future concerns are answered.

lessons.statement: Make room for understanding while following the responsibility that actually applies.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Keep workplace participation and formal duties distinct
intro.body:
A separate DHS team is discussing a draft communication practice. Priya waits for the supervisor to ask for concerns, while Cameron asks about a possible missing perspective during the explanation. Their responses do not establish a national profile or attitude toward leadership. A facilitator can clarify when input is invited and how it will be considered within the actual process. The learning question concerns understanding and participation, not a transfer of the decision role.

A supervisor’s title alone also does not establish every authority relevant to a longer-term change. Staff need the actual task, required review and applicable responsibility. DHS Equity Policy expects equity considerations in daily work and requires formal analysis for actions with prolonged or long-term impact scheduled for leadership approval, using the required toolkit or an appropriately developed tool. A friendly discussion or completed course does not substitute for that analysis.

The example supplies a distinct issue: supervisor Casey receives Jordan’s report that a coworker repeatedly says people from Jordan’s country should know their place and should not question managers. Jordan describes the remarks as national-origin harassment. Casey must not treat a power-distance concept as a reason to dismiss the allegation or ask Jordan to prove a cultural preference before the report proceeds.

Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report all protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. They must follow the actual agency complaint and investigation procedures, including any assigned authorized role. The policy prohibits retaliation. This exercise makes no finding about the actual conduct and authorizes no disciplinary decision.

Cultural inquiry and that reporting duty can be understood without confusing them. Casey may behave respectfully and explain the appropriate process, but optional learning, a private settlement or a group conversation cannot become a reporting prerequisite. A member’s quiet response also is not consent to the alleged remarks. The relevant process determines what happened and what response is appropriate.

Staff can practice the distinctions using this example without entering real personnel records or cultural histories. The consultant can provide guidance and feedback, while staff retain their own assigned equity work and actual obligations. Understanding a learned expectation is useful; it does not grant permission to disregard a required response.

items.title: Clarify how input is considered
items.body: The draft discussion needs an understandable invitation and an explanation of the process. Priya’s and Cameron’s responses alone do not establish motive or authority. Asking about the actual concern keeps the participation useful without making the group a substitute for the responsible decision-maker.

items.title: Report the allegation immediately
items.body: Jordan reports national-origin remarks about who may question managers. Casey’s role-specific duty is immediate reporting to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. The power-distance framework cannot decide the allegation, excuse the remarks or require a workshop before that duty is fulfilled.

items.title: Keep formal work within its scope
items.body: A longer-term communication change may require formal equity analysis and other actual review. This lesson can support a question about whose perspectives are considered, but it does not complete the analysis or create an approval. Staff should use the real applicable procedures rather than a course result as authorization.

tabs.label: An input question
tabs.body: The draft process can explain when staff contribute and how concerns are considered. That is different from profiling who is comfortable with authority. A particular question can inform the work even if the person’s personal history remains private and the decision responsibility stays where it actually belongs.

tabs.label: A protected-class allegation
tabs.body: The supplied national-origin allegation requires Casey’s immediate HR or agency Affirmative Action Officer report under Policy 1436. It cannot wait for a cultural interpretation exercise. The course should keep the duty explicit while leaving factual findings and the assigned response to the actual process.

tabs.label: A required decision process
tabs.body: A qualifying longer-term action requires the appropriate equity analysis and actual review. Questions about hierarchy may illuminate the process, but they do not satisfy every requirement or grant authority. A supportive conversation and a formal analysis are distinct kinds of work.

intro.heading: Recognize a changed exchange without ranking people
intro.body:
The final choir fiction supplies Lena’s and Bo’s accounts. Lena says the explicit question opportunity made it clear that clarification was welcome before singing. Bo says the question could be raised without guessing whether it would interrupt the explanation. Mira says the intended instruction was clarified and the sequence role remains the same. The later written correction is still being checked. No account from the rest of the choir is supplied.

Those facts describe a changed exchange that responded to particular learned meanings. They do not establish that Lena or Bo moved along a national power-distance scale, that every member felt included or that a single invitation caused permanent trust. Acknowledging the useful clarification does not require turning it into a universal success claim. Missing accounts remain unknown.

The conceptual learning is also more specific than “hierarchy is bad” or “authority must never be questioned.” The framework made expectations about respect and voice visible. The individual accounts then informed an invitation suited to this practice task. The actual sequencing responsibility and a useful opportunity to raise a question could coexist. Different facts or roles might call for another response.

A useful follow-up could check whether the unresolved written instruction has been clarified through the project’s actual arrangement. Another could invite a relevant experience from a willing member without asking for a cultural biography or rating everyone’s relationship to authority. A person may prefer not to discuss the exchange. That choice should not be converted into agreement, resistance or a score.

You may have learned something privately about your own relationship to speaking, waiting or being invited. Perhaps you now recognize consideration, responsibility or respect in an act you once interpreted differently. That self-understanding can stand alongside work application as a legitimate result. You need not share the reflection, produce a live change or declare a new stage to complete this course.

If you later apply the inquiry at work, keep the actual task, authority, evidence and duties clear. A cultural question is useful when it helps people understand and respond appropriately. It loses that value when it becomes a shortcut to personnel judgment or a reason to bypass the required process. Use the job aid to keep learned meanings, participation and responsibility connected.

items.title: Recognize the limited accounts
items.body: Lena and Bo describe why the explicit invitation helped this exchange. Those accounts are meaningful without representing every member. The unanswered written correction remains separate. Keeping both visible avoids inflating the result while retaining the clarification that actually occurred.

items.title: Keep the concept separate from a score
items.body: The case illustrates inquiry into expectations around unequal roles and respectful participation. It does not measure anyone’s orientation or establish movement on a national scale. The outcome depends on meanings the people describe and a particular invitation, not a classification of the contributors.

items.title: Value private understanding
items.body: You may recognize a familiar expectation in Ari’s example or understand Lena’s waiting differently. That insight can remain private and need not result in a work task. The example supports a complete learning route for anyone who does not wish to examine or disclose a personal memory.

tabs.label: An honest result
tabs.body: The particular invitation helped two members clarify the instruction, according to their supplied accounts. Mira’s stated sequencing role remained. This description keeps the useful result, the known responsibility and the open written question distinct without assigning other members an experience.

tabs.label: An inflated conclusion
tabs.body: Saying everyone now feels equal or all future concerns are solved would overstate the evidence. It also changes the aim from a fitting invitation to a universal promise. One exchange cannot establish every experience, a lasting cause or the elimination of every hierarchy.

tabs.label: A personal insight
tabs.body: A learner can understand why an invitation or waiting carried meaning without entering that memory. The insight is legitimate alongside an optional work application. It should not be judged by a public performance, a personal rating or a requirement to challenge every authority.

check.question: Which account fits the final fiction?
check.correct: The explicit invitation helped Lena and Bo clarify the instruction; Mira’s role and the unresolved written correction remain distinct.
wrong: Every member now has the same cultural values.
Private understanding has no value unless a work metric changes.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves the meanings the people describe, useful result and actual limits without ranking people or dismissing personal growth.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The example supplies no common-value finding for all members. The course measures no individual power-distance score. Private cultural understanding is legitimate without a work metric. Each alternative turns a limited learning account into a classification or imposes a condition the course does not require.

remember: Power distance concerns cultural expectations about unequal power; it is not a personal score or a judgment of worth.

sections.heading: Understand the expectation
items: Name the actual act or question before interpreting it: waiting, asking, agreeing or seeking clarification. Do not infer a cultural category from identity or appearance.
Invite the person’s meaning if appropriate without requiring a personal history. Use the Lena/Bo or Ari fiction for private learning.
Consider what respect, responsibility or consideration means in this particular relationship and context. Avoid making one response a universal rule.

sections.heading: Make participation and authority clear
items: Identify the actual task, responsible role and applicable process. A cultural expectation or confident manner does not create authority.
Consider an explicit, usable invitation that responds to the meanings the people describe. An opportunity to ask does not necessarily transfer the decision responsibility.
Keep an answered question, a recommendation under consideration and an unresolved concern distinct. Do not mark every issue resolved because the exchange was warm.

sections.heading: Recognize learning and preserve duties
items: Describe the limited result and the person’s account without assigning everyone the same experience or a cultural score. Missing feedback remains unknown.
Private self-understanding can remain unrecorded and worthwhile. A live change, public challenge or entered personal account is not required.

Use actual DHS equity-analysis and other agency procedures where applicable. Managers and supervisors must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under MMB Policy 1436; optional learning is not a gate.

sources.title: Hofstede: the dimensions of national culture
sources.note: The public definition of power distance concerns accepted and expected inequality of power among less powerful members. The national-culture comparison and within-country variation are distinct from an individual profile; no country scores are used.

sources.title: Hofstede: levels of analysis
sources.note: The brief explanation distinguishes individual, group and broader human levels. The course does not reproduce a linked research instrument or measure personal orientation.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Relevant sections explain personalized learned meanings, multiple affiliations, context and understanding oneself through encounters. The original choir and private-learning examples apply these concepts without predicting a group or requiring personal disclosure.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual daily equity responsibilities and formal analysis required for qualifying long-term actions remain separate from the learning exercise. A participation invitation does not replace the required toolkit or agency decision process.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: National-origin and other protected-class allegations retain immediate manager/supervisor reporting to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, agency procedures and nonretaliation protection. No finding or disciplinary authority is created by this course.
